lesson.menu_title: Speaking About the Future — Predictions, Plans and How Sure You Actually Are
lesson.menu_desc: Twelve words for what has not happened yet, and the stacking rule that carries likelihood and shape at once -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 15 -- Speaking About the Future
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Braulio Zemel | Lesson 15 -- Speaking About the Future

listenings.text: Three things on the year ahead, and then I will hand back to you. First, growth. Growth will probably have slowed by the middle of the year, and I want to be precise about that word probably, because I am not telling you it is certain. Second, the direction. The direction is inevitable at this point, in the sense that the momentum is already there and nobody in any government is going to reverse it. What is genuinely uncertain is the timing, and it may stay uncertain for another two years, which is an uncomfortable thing to say on the radio. And third, a piece of advice that costs you nothing. If somebody gives you a date and a number in the same sentence, stop listening. One of the two will be wrong, and it will take the other one down with it.

When somebody who has learned English makes a prediction, the tense is almost always right. What is missing is something else entirely. It is the degree of certainty. In Portuguese, and in most languages, the voice carries that: the same words said two different ways are two different claims, and everybody in the room hears the difference. English puts it in the words instead. So there are levels, and they are worth learning as a set. It could be, which is a possibility you are not betting on. It might well be, which is a strong possibility you would take seriously. And it will probably be, which is where you are willing to be quoted. Three degrees, three sets of words. And this matters much more abroad than it does at home, because a written sentence, or one said over a bad connection, keeps every word and loses every bit of the voice. Anything you were carrying in your tone alone arrives flattened.

extra_audio.text: Diane says that in thirty years of long-range planning she was never paid to be right, only to be useful early. She explains that a prediction is a single answer while a forecast is a range with the reasoning attached, so that somebody can argue with it. She describes what she actually says when people ask her what will happen: two scenarios, one bet, and the condition that would make her wrong. Braulio admits that he has only ever made predictions and then defended them. Diane gives him a last habit, which is never to predict a date and a size in the same sentence.
